For fixed n, j^α a_(n,j)≤1 and tends to 1, which verifies the frozen weak-norm equality and strong nonmembership at αp≤1. For the frozen regularly varying limits, near X/(nt)=1 use uniform regular variation, while on the exponentially small complement and j in a bounded rescaled interval the log of the ratio is O(log(nt)) uniformly, by monotonicity and polynomial bounds on the weights. For larger j use a_(n,j)≤w_j and the Potter majorant; choose its exponent so the pth power is integrable. This verifies the frozen leading equivalents. The narrowed claim was audited afresh: on |X−m|≤m/2 expand log(1+(X−m)/(j+m)) through the cubic, with error bounded by C|X−m|^4/(j+m)^4. The third centered moment is O(m) and the fourth O(m²); the complementary relative logarithm is O(log m) uniformly in j, with exponential probability. The resulting uniform relative error O(m^−2) sums absolutely at s=αp>1 with total error O(m^(−s−1)). The trapezoidal half-endpoint term and the variance contribution combine exactly to −(1+st)/(2(1+s)); j=1 independently yields −α(1+t)/2 in the normalized operator norm. Expanding each leading term at m+d verifies the two different effective additive shifts. The frozen NumPy/SciPy file was inspected, not executed. The new standard-library /workspace/repairs/5/verify.py was successfully run; ten finite parameter choices check both coefficients with an analytic tail bracket up to floating-point rounding. The infinite proof does not depend on the diagnostics.

value.rationale: The surviving contribution is not the already available leading law or a cosmetic rate rewrite. At the canonical exact-power ideal threshold model, the correction resolves how the positive binomial variance contribution and negative discrete summation correction compete, yields a sharp signed bias of the first-order mass approximation, and shows that the norm and finite-p mass require different time shifts. The uniform control over singular rank required to get the mass error makes it more than a fixed-coordinate Taylor computation. The corrected result is useful for precision estimates of the same canonical orbit without claiming a new general regular-variation theorem.
